Chapter 8: Expanding Possibility Through Play and Experimentation.
You know that feeling after you’ve pushed through the hardest part of a big change? The initial discomfort starts to fade, and suddenly, there’s this new spark. A sense of curiosity. Maybe even a little excitement.
That’s the perfect moment to start experimenting. Now, life isn’t about getting everything right on the first try. What if you could treat your day-to-day like a series of experiments? Imagine becoming the scientist of your own life—testing out ideas, seeing what sticks, and adjusting as you go.
Here’s the cool part—when you start thinking this way, setbacks aren’t scary anymore. They just become data points. Things to learn from, not failures to fear.
So, how do you actually build this playful, experimental mindset? Let’s break it down:
First, try what’s called “safe-to-fail” experiments. These are simple actions where the risks are low, but the rewards can surprise you. Maybe you strike up a conversation with someone new, pick up a hobby you’ve never tried, or suggest a small tweak at work. The outcome? Totally uncertain—and that’s the point.
Next, track your results. It doesn’t have to be fancy. Just jot down what you tried, how it felt, and anything you noticed. Over time, you’ll spot patterns—what lights you up, what doesn’t, and where you want to go next.
Most importantly, celebrate your effort, not just the result. Every time you step out of your comfort zone, give yourself some credit. That’s how you build confidence and keep your spirit of exploration alive.
Here’s a helpful way to look at it: think about a child learning to walk. There are tumbles and stumbles, sure. But with every fall, they gather new information and get just a little bit stronger. It’s messy, but it always leads to progress.
When you embrace experimentation like this, you start to realize that the world isn’t as rigid as it seems. Suddenly, it feels a lot more like a playground, and a lot less like a test you have to pass.
So, why not give yourself permission to play, to experiment, and to discover what’s truly possible?
